frames.narration: Checkout handles 50,000 requests per second. Its request counter has labels route (20), status (5) and region (6): at most 20 x 5 x 6 = 600 series, about 1.8 MB at 3 KB each.
Someone adds customer_id as a label. With 1,000,000 customers the bound becomes 600 x 1,000,000 = 600 million series, about 1.8 TB. The metrics store runs out of memory.

The fix: keep only bounded labels on the metric (back to 600 series) and put customer_id on the span and log line, where cost scales with events. An exemplar on the slow latency bucket carries one trace id, so a dashboard spike links to a real trace.

Keeping every trace is 50,000 x 5 KB = 250 MB/s, about 21.6 TB a day. Head sampling at 1% hashes the trace id: 500 traces/s kept, about 216 GB a day, and every service makes the same decision for the same trace.
The catch: 0.2% of requests fail, that is 100 error traces per second, and a 1% head sample keeps only 1 of them per second. The other 99 are gone before anyone knew they were errors.

Tail sampling: the sampler buffers every span of each trace for a 30 s decision wait (1.5 million traces, about 7.5 GB), then keeps all errors, all traces slower than 800 ms (1% of traffic) and 1% of the rest: about 1,100 traces/s, 2.2% of traffic.

Now every trace has a weight. A kept error or slow trace stands for 1 request; a kept ordinary trace stands for 100. In one second about 494 ordinary + 600 interesting traces give 494 x 100 + 600 = 50,000 requests (the ordinary count varies by roughly 22 either way, so the estimate by about 4%).

Without weights, the p99 of the kept traces would be several times too high, because slow traces were over-kept. Use exact metric counters for counts and rates, and weighted traces for examples and estimates.
